texts: mixed: the generic fires per child and the names and the lantern-stations are all there, but "by heart" was taken literally and became a by-phrase on "heart", an atom that says nothing downstream. Say it in one verb instead: "Children memorize the names of the lantern-stations."
good. a fireable per-child rule with the station names as what is chanted and "in games" kept as its own phrase rather than a place.
good. a fireable per-Keeper rule with "often" recorded both as a lowered strength and as the quantifier word, each Keeper marrying into their own fisher family.

bad: "outside a Keeper family" was read as "outside one particular Keeper family", so the rule fires for a Keeper who married inside one Keeper family but outside some other one, awarding the station in cases you did not mean. Drop the article so the phrase names the kind rather than a single family: "A Keeper who marries outside Keeper families keeps the station."
good. the permission distributes to every Keeper's child and the "of any Keeper" restriction is kept as a condition of the rule rather than dropped.

bad: "may" over a kind should become a standing permission attached to the kind, but "a Keeper's child" offers no kind symbol to attach it to, so it came out as an event rule carrying the permission form reserved for one-off acts by an individual. Name the kind directly, exactly as your later sentence already does: "Keeper children may decline apprenticeship."
good. "some" mints a set, and both the set-level denial and the per-member denial are emitted, so neither the group nor any individual is asserted to apprentice.

mixed: the three trades and the group of children all land in a fireable rule, but one "often" spread over three verbs left the frequency word itself unrecorded (there is one slot for it and three verbs competing for it), and "down the coast" loses its along-the-coast sense. One finite clause per trade fixes both: "Some of those children fish, some farm in the Hollows, and some trade on the coast."
